doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

chapter: Hearing the bands and the rhythm guitar ideal
title: Guitar amplification, Django, and his rhythm guitar idols
summary: Freddie Green and amplification, Oscar Moore, Christian, Django; he wanted to be a rhythm guitarist like Reuss, Bryan, Condon and Green.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: So the idea of amplification for the guitar, I know Freddie Green was never really amplified right? He just kind of would basically feel that sound.

Not that I know of. He once went out and they got him a mic and an amp or something, but it was never used, and later on I heard that you know when Bobby Hackett played with Glenn Miller, Glenn Miller had him, Bobby didn’t have to carry it, the band boy had to carry an amp all over the place, but Bobby never used it, he didn’t like it. And no, of course we heard Oscar Moore, that was a hot ticket then, the King Cole Trio was the hot ticket, and we all had those, you know all the kids had those records and we’d listen to them, and of course we knew about the Benny Goodman Sextet with Charlie Christian, all the guys had that, and they were on Columbia I think, yeah. I can remember the labels, you know and stuff. But somehow that never got to me. It’s like I loved Django Reinhardt. For one part of my youth I had every Django Reinhardt I could get my hands on. But I never, for some reason, it never occurred to me that I wanted to do that. And I later on, funny, I had so many friends who were really into Django. One guy in Cleveland he said, “I used to tie my fingers, put rubber bands around my fingers to try to ape Django’s two fingers” you know that two finger typing technique that he played with. And I mean guys, I know several that were Django freaks, they can play everything by Django. They lived Django, they think Django, and of course later on I found in Paris, in Europe, there are hundreds of them that do Django, with varying degrees of success. But for some reason, I don’t think I ever felt, first of all, for some damn reason that I can’t understand, I wanted to be a rhythm guitar player at first. And in fact, managed to be just that. And set as my idols, those guys like Allan Reuss, and Mike Bryan and Eddie Condon and Freddie Green and whoever else I could think of. All those guys, and trumpet players and horn players would tell me, “Those are the guys” they would say, “those are the guys. They don’t show off, they don’t need to take choruses and stuff, but they play for the band. That’s a team thing.” And of course in a sense they were absolutely right. Because there is a symbiosis that happens between rhythm players, when they get tight and when it really starts to work, that you can’t get as a soloist really, at least I’ve never been able to. It doesn’t feel quite the same. It’s a special feeling. And a friend of mine called me up just three days, four days ago, he’s an amateur guitarist and a collector in Texas. and he called me up and he said, he’d been playing electric guitar all his life and he said he had a teacher, and in Texas he signed up for a course. They have a 23-piece big band, and you sign up for a course. You pay money and you work in the big band. They do Basie and Glenn Miller and stuff like that. And he said “I really had to play rhythm guitar. And my teacher said, ‘You know, it will hurt for a while, but you’ll get to the next plateau and you’ll play, even though it hurts you’ll play, and then all of a sudden you’ll find out it doesn’t hurt anymore.’” I guess it’s like anything physical: © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
